# Introduction

The aim was to see how effective simple temperature monitoring of the four ports on a typical 4 port buffer installation is.   Ian kindly offered his series 3 as a unit for this testing. This is a living document and is subject to change until the end of the experiment.

See the photographs in the Appendix.

* 16 kW unit \- series 3, 3055 software  
* 28mm primaries, about 12m away from the cylinder  
* Hysteresis, type 0 (\+ 2 °C)  
* Pump Capacity 100% (\~ 33 litres/min)  
* Pump Operation in heating : On 2, Off 1  
* Weather compensation 45°C,25°C at \-3°C,15°C  (Target \= 41.7 \- 1.1 x Outside)  
* Using outlet water temperature as control  
* Worldheat cylinder, integrated buffer  
* Radiators \- controlled via 1 thermostat set at 21°C, Wilo Ku 25/8 SC pump \- constant curve III.    
* UFH heating \- 3 loops, controlled via 2 thermostats, Grundfos UPS 25-60 pump \- not sure of speed setting and thermal mixing valve (set at 45°C).  Thermostats set to 20°C  
* UFH loops probably have wide spacing.  
* Night time the radiator and UFH thermostats are set to 18°C

# Initial Considerations

This configuration will not be pure weather compensation and will suffer from stop/start heating demands from the thermostats.  Given the 3 zones, and any radiator TRV’s opening/closing, then the flow rates on the heating side will be very unpredictable.   With AI settings in use during a heating demand then the actual changing target also makes analysis more complex.

With an overnight setback via external thermostats then the expectation is that the heating would immediately switch off at the setback time \- on the basis that the setback temperature will be below the current temperature.  Therefore there will be heat loss overnight until the setback is reached, or the setback period ends and new higher target temperatures are used.  This lack of heating will result in the heat pump having to work harder to recover that lost heat, so the system efficiency will most certainly be compromised.  In addition, the use of thermostats set to near target temperature defeats the purpose of weather compensation and will cause the LG to potentially switch off, or cycle due to much reduced demand due to individual zone/radiators closing.  Given the problematic start up of LG ThermaV’s (high power output for the first \~10 minutes before modulating) then this will also lower the COP.

## Requirements  

From Ian \- 14th Nov: *So let me bring in a quirk of our home life. Upstairs we have a study, it gets quite a lot of use by my wife for WFH. The upstairs on the whole is naturally about 2c lower than downstairs (where the Tado controller is set to 20.5c acting as a limiter). If we leave the home to run as we usually do but with no setback it's too warm in the bedrooms for sleeping but we can't lower the TRVs or the WC or fixed temp during the day as my wife gets too cold at her desk.*

In this situation it may be better to have the TRV’s all open \- and to use the lock shields to have the maximum flow rate to the study, and the other rooms having lower flow rates.  In principle this is a reasonable approach, but to achieve this in practice may take some considerable time, as is the case in any balancing situation.

# First Data Capture

The 4-port monitor was configured initially for Ian’s WiFi network before dispatch and emoncms feeds were created to receive the data.  Ian confirmed data was collected and then connected the 4 temperature probes to his VCyl buffer tank pipework.

## Initial Run \- 11th Nov

Started collecting 4 temperatures at \~ 11am, 10th November.  After overnight run through to \~9am 11th November:  
![][image2]  
Without actual on/off data it is more challenging to begin to interpret this but:

* The heating return is relatively stable, but very low.  
* The LG return is tracking the LG outlet but not as responsive as seen in other Vcyl buffers.  The return is also significantly lower than expected during the DHW cycle.  Is the thermocouple on the return to the LG or just from the buffer and getting some thermal pick up from DHW ?  
* Exponential decays are indicative of pumps off on either side of the buffer.  For example the clear fall of the heating flow temp from \~9pm through to 5:30 am heating again.  There is the LG cycling period from \~3pm until 5pm \- will zoom in later.  
* The wide DT on the heating side suggests it is running at least half the flow rate of the LG water pump, but I suspect that this is an artefact of very poor mixing in the buffer.  
* Equally, the relatively large DT on the LG side may be due to mixing effects.  There are lots of experiments to try and uncover the mysteries here.

## Details

At the start of this behaviour then the flow temperature decays away with the exponential fall indicative of no demand.

The subsequent peaks are spaced at around 8 minute intervals.  Clearly some very short duration heating.  Difficult to see here whether this is due to thermostat activity, perhaps precariously balanced on a set point or the LG switching off.  Given the final sustained rise above the previous short cycle peaks then it suggests thermostat behaviour.  But not 100% certain that this is the case.  The LG data log would be able to identify whether it was the demand signal or not.

This next period, immediately following the rapid cycles above probably shows some modulated behaviour.  After the initial flow temperature peak, which took \~ 12 minutes to achieve, then the power output looks to have fallen so the flow temperature reduces then picks back up again as the likelihood is that LG increased power.  This is observed in other LG units when this ‘wave’ kind of pattern emerges.  Just after 14-30 then the cycle stops, possibly the heating demand signal ends.  And it restarted some 9 minutes later.  This time the cycle stopped 9 minutes later and more likely due to LG target being met \- flow was at 34°C at the time, so suggesting an outdoor temperature of \~ 9°C. 

This period shows these shorter cycles, with some ‘kinks’ in the flow temperatures that are associated with flat periods of the LG return temperature.  Maybe induced by pump behaviour both on the LG side (due to the pump setting in heating, 2 minute on and 1 minute off) and the thermostat controlled secondary side.

At 17:21 the system stops, and the temperatures gradually fall away until some activity at 18:23.  I would guess that this is just a water pump cycle which the LG will perform when no heat demand is present.  There are settings that control when the water pump will be energised, and maybe that is set to 1 hour, or the LG activates the pump briefly in any event.  This short burst pulls a bit of warmer water from the pipework/buffer resulting in this effect.

After this (likely) water pump burst then there could be further water pump only activity but there is certainly some heating starting at 19:40 with the rise from 28°C to 38°C.  It may modulate down perhaps, or more likely hit the target and the compressor cycle stopped, the temperature then falling back to 35.6°C and a restart.  Followed quickly by another off phase and then up to the final heating before the DHW cycle starts at the end of this chart.

The DHW cycle took about half an hour, with the flow temperature climbing from \~ 33°C to 58°C in that period. Note that the return temperature is significantly below the flow temperature, despite not flowing through the buffer.    The peak return temperature was only \~ 42°C.

Maybe the temperature probe hasn’t been attached to the heat pump return and is just seeing temperature rise due to thermal conductivity from the actual heat pump return onto the buffer heat pump return ?

Overnight there was a rise in the LG flow and corresponding fall in the LG return.  This may be again as a result of a short LG water pump operation, or a thermal siphon kind of effect where warmer water causes some displacement in the buffer.

(some evidence of loss of data, possibly due to low WiFi signal strength).  
The system was set for a UFH zone to activate at 3-30, the other zone at 4-30 and then the radiators at 5-30am

![][image3]

It is self-evident that the LG did not respond at 3-30 or 4-30, and there didn’t appear to be any heating pump activity on the heating side at those times either.   It may be that the temperatures for the thermostats to engage at 3-30 and 4-30 were simply too low and therefore no heating demand occurred.

Presumably the radiator controlled zone signalled at the heat pump started, and after \~ 15 minutes the LG looks to have successfully modulated down.  The gently rising flow and return temperature for the next half hour or so would occur in a well balanced system if the heat pump was slightly overpowering the property.  However, these temperatures and possible flow rate of 34 l/min suggest a relatively high power output, perhaps 11 kW but that may be reasonable given the property having to warm up due to no heating during the colder overnight period of \~ 9 hours (i.e. the average kWh would be much lower than a sustained 11 kWh).

## Initial Thoughts

The system is not behaving in a predictable manner and needs some experimentation to determine what exactly is happening.  Any investigation with heating systems generally takes time due to the thermal mass of the property, especially without additional monitoring equipment.

The buffer is without doubt a problem, and that is not unique to this particular install.  The oblate geometry and flow rates that vary significantly will result in complex fluid dynamics within the vessel that destroy any thermal stratification.

The following questions, and Ian’s responses helped guide the next steps.

1. What are the pump pre-run/post-run times (if on 3055\) ?  *1 minute on/off*  
2. Any idea of heat loss ?  What does the Heat Geek quote indicate (is the property description accurate) ? *14.2 kW (PW, HG suggests 11.1 kW)*  
3. What do the flow meters show on the UFH manifold when:  
   1. No demand : *0*  
   2. Rads only : *0*  
   3. Zone 1 only (no rads) : *4*  
   4. Zone 2 only (no rads) : *4,4*  
   5. Zone 1 \+ 2 only (no rads) : *4,4,4*  
   6. All active, UFH \+ rads : *4,4,4*  
4. What speed setting is the Grundfos set to ? *Max speed 3*  
5. Does the UFH pump only turn on when a UFH zone calls for heat ?  Does it actually turn on at all ? *yes, it works as expected*  
6. Does activating UFH only cause the LG to start a heating cycle ? Yes, will start the HP.   
7. Do the zone valves open and close according to the radiator/UFH thermostat demands ? *Yes, when the UFH thermostat is calling the flow meters work and the pump switches on. It is separate from RADS from what I have seen over time.. I think when it turns on it also turns on the RADS pump (not sure about this really, I would assume this shouldn’t happen because the rads don’t need the heat when just the UFH is calling for it sometimes.)*  
8. Are the temperature probes for the heat pump on the pipework before the diverter valve for the flow, and after the tee from the cylinder and buffer for the LG return ? *I believe so yes, please see pic for placement. It looks like one of the probes fell out (Heating return), I have now placed it better at 11.10am on 13/11/2025*  
9. When the system is in a relatively steady state \- do the LG reported inlet and outlet temperatures align with those reported by the ‘gadget’ ?  
10. What are the Tank Setting 1, Tank Setting 2 and DHW Time Setting values ? *TS1 5/55, TS2 3/DHW, TS1 5/55, DTS 45/30/30*  
11. For the overnight test with the UFH zones on at 3-30, 4-30 and rads at 5-30, what temperatures were set ?  *Setback for UFH is at 19c, Rads are at 18c. I note that the home has not dropped below those levels for the last few weeks. It should mean no heating is called because the limit is not reached.*

# Gadget Issues \- 15th Nov

From the data collected it was very difficult to reconcile the behaviour.  Ian checked the connectivity of the DS18B20 probes and It appeared that some had been inadvertently positioned on incorrect pipework and in some cases the probe had detached from the pipe.

Using jubilee clips a more robust solution for temporarily positioning these probes.  And a test after installation of the probes to ensure they are working as expected would save some time.

The following shows a relatively long cycle with UFH heating only, targeting a fixed outlet of 40°C. Ian stated that only 2 UFH loops were running at the time, and obviously no radiators \- so there would be losses to unheated areas.    
![][image4]

Between 11:50 and 12:25, where it looks like the system would be running then we see that the LG flow/return temperatures are gradually falling, this is indicative of the heat loss being too high.  The average statistics for that period, assuming an LG flow rate of 34 l/min are (where Q\_l is the calculated flow on the load side).

| LG Flow °C | LG Return °C | LG kW | Load Flow °C | Load Return °C | Q\_l l/min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 37.4 \+ 0.7 | 35.7 *\+* 0.5 | 3.8 | 35.7 \+ 0.4 | 31.1 \+ 0.2 | 12.6 |

This leads to the calculated buffer mixing view, with the LG source on the left hand side and the load on the right.

Here 9.2 l/min of the LG flow is being mixed with 3.4 l/min of return water from the UFH.  24.8 l/min of the LG flow is being passed to its inlet. 

The flow setters show \~ 4 l/min, they are not terribly accurate so this 12.6 l/min is not an unreasonable result.

This would have an average temperature in the floor loops of 33.4°C, outdoor temperature was around 11°C.  The system was then switched to radiator only mode, again targeting a fixed outlet temperature of 33.4°C.

![][image5]  
   
Following the switch on surge then modulation occurred, then we see the LG temperature gradually increasing suggesting the property is overpowering slightly.  Of course we have no view of the house temperatures so we would expect the internal temperature to be rising here.

Between 14:10 and 15:05 the average data was:

| LG Flow °C | LG Return °C | LG kW | Load Flow °C | Load Return °C | Q\_l l/min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 37.3 \+ 0.4 | 32.9 *\+* 0.4 | 9.7 | 33.0 \+ 0.5 | 31.0 \+ 0.5 | 74.8 |

This has produced a very high flow rate on the heating side, something that is unlikely.  The buffer network would be as shown.

This high power output is driven by the extremely high flow rate on the secondary side.  So it would be good to look at changing the Wilo settings to see the impact.

## Suggestions 15/11/25

* Open all TRV’s and set the stats very high, so LG is always in heat demand  
* Set fixed heating to 40°C and run for a few days gathering 6 hour averages if possible  
* Change the Wilo from constant pressure to proportional pressure mode

## Further Areas/Improvements

* Reduce the UFH pump speed to widen the DT a little and may balance out better  
* LG settings \- capacity/hysteresis/inlet/pump in heating/silent  
* Radiator rebalancing

# Post Install Correction Data Collection

With the probes in the correct position and returned data more in line with expectations then further data capture was performed as changes were made to the system.

## 16th Nov \- Load Pump Changes

The Wilo pump constant pressure mode was switched to its proportional pressure 2 setting.  The aim being to allow the system to respond more appropriately to TRV’s closing where the pump would reduce flow rate accordingly instead of increasing flow rate to maintain head pressure.  Also to see whether any possible reduction in flow rates would result in widening the deltaT.  And finally the proportional pressure modes will slightly reduce electricity consumption.

Further changes were made over a few hours to see the impact of moving to proportional pressure 1 mode, and to switch the Grundfos UFH to its speed setting II.  
![][image6]

The initial change to the Wilo pump from Constant Pressure 3 to Proportional Pressure 2 seemed stable for a period, but then temperatures became unstable,  Given the fall and subsequent fast peak could have been due to a DHW cycle starting so there would have been no source active for the heating cycle.  The fall at 12pm is probably the LG switching off \- difficult to be sure without modbus or logging information.

Switching the UFH pump from speed 3 to speed 2 may have had a detrimental effect. Prior to the change the system seems to be overloading the property at current conditions, but following the change then possibly under-powering.  However, it may have been due to LG modulating further following the period of rising temperatures.

The UK is about to enter a cold spell so this will be a more challenging time for the property, but there should be less likelihood of the LG stopping as the load will be higher.  
![][image7]  
This shows the system performing reasonably well after the combined pump changes, with the Wilo set on the lower PP1 setting as it appeared to re-establish itself following that change at \~ 2pm.   The disturbance at \~5-30pm was due to a DHW cycle.  Note after that cycle that the system failed to achieve the target, indeed the target of 40°C has not been reached for some time \- but this may simply be due to the offset between the LG sensors and the DS18B20’s.  There appears to be an overall shift downwards after that DHW cycle.   Need to check the values recorded by the LG to compare with the probe data.  
    
At 9pm Ian reduced the radiator thermostat to 19°C and the LG didn’t restart a heating cycle until \~10-15,  Then the rapid cycling occurs as the only load will be on the UFH and the system cannot cope at such reduced levels.  The reason for setting the radiator thermostat to 19°C was due to the property being too warm.  The fixed heating target was reduced to 35°C to determine whether the system could modulate with lower temperatures.

## Silent Mode Operation

![][image8]

Running overnight from 17th, with silent mode enabled from 11-30pm to 5-30am,  during near freezing conditions, the system performed reasonably well.  Good recovery from the defrosts.  The highlighted regions show where DHW cycles were performed, with the end of the cycle evident with the spike behaviour.  The water pumps on the heating side continue to operate, so the return water from the heating system is recirculated.  It will most likely be better to simply stop the pumps via the external pump relay and let thermal decay set in, as opposed to pumping.  

The house did lose temperature in these conditions, so the 35°C flow temperature at \~1 outside is too aggressive and needs raising.  7°C deg outside, 35°C flow \- maybe a little cool, the flow temperature was increased to 39°C with outdoor temperature \~ 6°C just before 2pm.

This steady state is delivering perhaps 9 kW at the outdoor conditions, and holding steady with no apparent increase or decrease in heating side temperatures.  This indicates a heat loss of \~ 600W/°C \- 13.8 kW for design temperatures of \-2°C outside and 21°C inside.  

The DT at 4pm was 4.7°C on the LG side and 2.1°C on heating (implies heating flowing 2.2x quicker than the LG)

Temperatures are expected to fall again overnight, but the experiment will continue with the following settings:

Radiators, thermostat set to 25°C for 05:30 to 20:00, and to 15°C during the ‘off’ phase.  When in the off phase then silent mode will be active.  Underfloor thermostat set to 25°C and continuous operation.  The flow temperature was increased to 39°C at 2pm.

So the initial question will be how the system copes with the lower UFH only load during this period.

12am on the 18th to 12pm on the 19th showed the following (note the flow temperature increase at 2pm, this was also evident on the previous chart).

![][image9]  
The overnight run shows drop outs due to defrosts and DHW, but there were also 2 periods where the heating demand stopped \- so the UFH controller disabled heating.  This somewhat negates the overnight run, but there are clear periods of potential cycling, but difficult to be completely sure when only temperature data is available.

Ian discovered that the UFH was having problems with connectivity and this was causing drop out, so remedial action was taken to try and resolve the issue at least temporarily,

The radiator thermostat logging showed the loss of temperature overnight and then the recovery throughout the day. 

## Pump Capacity Change \- 19th November

The pump capacity was reduced to 90% at \~2-15 pm as part of the efforts to reduce consumption slightly and to see if this helped the LG achieve modulation.  And at 9pm the flow temperature was increased to 40°C.

![][image10]  
The effect of the pump capacity isn’t particularly clear \- and the visual flow meter is too dirty to see actual flow rate clearly.  What we can see is that overnight there didn’t appear to be any loss of UFH heating and the unit possibly managed to modulate for the period with only the defrosts at 11pm and \~4am evident.  The DT on LG at \~3am was 2°C and 3.7°C on the UFH, indicating the floor running UFH running around 54% of the LG’s flow rate.

## CH14 \- 20th November

The flow temperature was increased to 45°C at 9am \- the downstairs areas were warm but cooler upstairs.  Obviously with the UFH active all night then heating would clearly benefit downstairs, with the upstairs also gaining some heating.  This is where the benefit of keeping all of the property warm can be seen \- the house would be more stable and not necessarily require the boost to 45°C.  Of course night-time temperatures may then be uncomfortable and that is the trade off.

However, at 11-15am the system had a CH14 flow rate error.  This was somewhat surprising as the assumption has been that the LG is keeping a fixed flow rate based on capacity.  But CH14 indicates that flow rate has dropped below the 15 l/min threshold.  It may have been a complete co-incidence with the capacity change made yesterday, but certainly very suspicious.  This really illustrates the need to determine how the series 3 LG’s modulate their flow rates \- and this may depend on controller software, or motherboard version.  So the capacity was increased back to 100%.

The radiator thermostat was set to 23°C for 4am to 8pm, and 19°C for the remaining time.

![][image11]

So possibly the radiator thermostat called for heat around 4am, causing the cold radiator water to rapidly drop the return temperature.

The question here is whether during the night periods with UFH only whether the LG is managing to modulate or is switching off ?

## Confusing Artefacts

![][image16]

* Here the UFH only is on in an overnight period \- and the cycles are about 16m apart.  The peak to trough on the flow is only 2.4°C \- the hysteresis should be 4°C band, so why the reduced amplitude ?  The assumption is that the LG isn’t modulating here but cycling.  
* If the LG is cycling then we could reasonably expect that the LG’s flow and return would be similar \- arguably the cooler inlet could pick up residual heat in the LG’s heat exchanger and would then cool during the pipe run back to the buffer.  But the offset here is pronounced.

* Similarly in defrosts we see the LG flow fall but on occasion not below the LG return.  It crosses the heating flow \- almost that the sensors are incorrectly labelled.

Ian noted on the morning of 25th November that since the electrician visited one of the UFH loops had not been active. This was corrected by resetting the thermostat.  Then really odd behaviour occurred overnight, coupled with a loss of data.

![][image17]  
This inversion of the LG return temperature above the flow temperature makes zero sense.  And the following day the pattern repeated and is consistent with the radiator demand stopping.

![][image18]

This is pretty baffling and maybe is the result of some thermo-siphoning taking place ?  The LG data here would be really useful to see what temperatures it is measuring at its inlet and outlet, when the compressor is on and whether the thermostat was calling or not.  Check valves on the buffer flow pipes would stop any reverse flow so that would be a recommended change.

When Ian returns from holiday and this event occurs again then the data log may provide some helpful information \- on the 27th November data set (27th to 28th) system response was:

![][image19]  
At 8pm then the likelihood was that the stats stopped calling for heat.  The odd effect at 10pm may have been the result of a DHW cycle where a plug of hot water from that heating session propagated to the buffer.  Only having temperature data and not useful heat energy data makes analysis difficult.

During the 1pm to 8pm interval then there was this apparent cycling \- but the amplitude of the LG flow temperature was very low, so not clear how such a low amplitude of heating would arise given the hysteresis settings.  

## Overnight 4th December

Ian has returned from his trip and the overnight behaviour from the 4th to the 5th showed

![][image20]

Looking in more detail from the period following 9pm and using the LG data log we can see a little more clearly what may be happening.

![][image21]  
Between the DHW cycle completing and the start of AI mode heating at 02:26 then the return temperatures show some spike behaviours.  There were no calls to heating at this stage, and the heating flow didn’t show any response \- so unlikely to be directly being pumped at least. Unexplained behaviour at this stage.

Then it appears that there were 4 short on/off cycles.  The flow temperature is significantly below the AI target temperature at an estimated 45°C.  Also note that the LG flow temperature does not align well during these periods, for example the first ‘off’ at 02:30 the LG recorded inlet and outlet temperatures of 20°C and 30°C.  The 30°C does not seem achievable from this view.  These short cycles may be due to the thermostat hovering around a set point perhaps ?  Poor behaviour either way.

After the 04:10 defrost then the system remained active and the flow temperature climbed upwards \- being interrupted during the process by the defrost activity.  So this would have introduced a lot of heat loss overnight.

After 06:32 defrost then a DHW cycle kicked in, with the DHW temperature at 42°C compared to its target 47°C (from the LG log).  The data log showed the next event as the defrost at 07:20 \- the DHW temperature in the log was 45°C \- a disappointing increase of 3°C, but it may have coincided with morning showers etc.  After this defrost then normal heating continued.

# Recommendations

* Introduce LG modbus monitoring, or at least get electricity consumption data into emoncms.  
* Add a distribution header or similar such that not all flow has to be through the Wilo.  
* Add a check valve on the buffer flow pipes to prevent any reverse thermosiphon effect  
* Re-pipe the buffer in a 3 pipe configuration with the return through the buffer.  
* Use the LG external relay and contactors to stop the recirculating pumps when the LG is in a DHW cycle.  
* Switch to LG control, to provide better setback/boost ability.  The use of the external pump relay will be useful in this scenario.  
* Thermostats shouldn’t be used to control the LG, only to act as a last resort in terms of temperature control (overheat).  
* Replace the older Grunfos pump with a more efficient equivalent \- i.e. instead of consuming 50W may be less than 15W.  
* New UFH heating centre & 2 new stats  
* Power monitoring the Wilo to try and get some flow estimates.   
* Increase to 35 or 42 mm primaries

# 

# Final Reflections

From the author’s perspective this experiment has highlighted a few issues that are important to consider for any remote monitoring/analysis perspective.

* Whilst the temperature data on its own is a useful tool, and when running well is an excellent guide \- but the lack of other information, such as when external thermostats may be calling for heat and when DHW cycles are active makes analysis so much harder.  
* The lack of at least one accurate flow rate compounds the analysis problem from a power generation and efficiency perspective.  
* Having TRV’s and UFH zones coming in/out at various times means steady state is obviously difficult to establish, and secondly makes analysis difficult.  
* Living with a system whilst experiments are ongoing to try and optimise and evaluate the effect of changes is difficult.  Such changes are hopefully required over a short period \- but they are disruptive and the property can be over/under heated and costs may be higher as the settings are modified.  
* Some method to ensure that the gadget is monitoring the correct pipework would be useful, to avoid confusion.   
* Better method of strapping the probes to the pipework.  Metal jubilee clips are the most obvious.  No experiments have been performed to assess the advantage of using them.  
* Adding external temperature data should be added to the gadget data collection.


The 4-pipe buffer continues to show poor behaviour.  It would be interesting to run more of these experiments on different systems but it does require the homeowner to be ‘engaged’ with the process.  Or a single site visit would probably show similar behaviour in a few hours of high temperature run time.  

The advantage of the simple temperature probe monitoring is that it is the least invasive of any other solution.  No access to the LG required or other equipment \- just reasonable access to the pipework, mains power for a USB charger and reasonable WiFi connectivity.  And it does show cycling behaviour and the mixing effects within the buffer so it is a valuable tool in isolation.  LG modbus data is of course easily available and the gadget supports it, but an external modbusTCP adapter is required.  And the homeowner needs to be a bit more tech-savvy to configure it, and of course it needs connecting physically to the LG.
